passages.t: Hezekiah goes into the house of the LORD
passages.happening:
‘On hearing this report, King Hezekiah tore his clothes, put on sackcloth, and entered the house of the LORD’ (verse 1). He sends Eliakim, Shebna and the leading priests, all in sackcloth, to the prophet Isaiah (verse 2). ‘Today is a day of distress, rebuke, and disgrace; for children have come to the point of birth, but there is no strength to deliver them’ (verse 3). Perhaps the LORD will hear the words of the Rabshakeh, sent ‘to defy the living God’ (verse 4), and rebuke him. Pray for the remnant that is left.

Isaiah answers: ‘Do not be afraid of the words you have heard’ (verse 6). God will put a spirit in the king of Assyria, so that he hears a rumor and returns home, where he will fall by the sword (verse 7).

The Rabshakeh finds the king of Assyria fighting at Libnah (verse 8). Sennacherib hears that Tirhakah king of Cush is coming to fight him (verse 9), and sends Hezekiah another message: do not let your God deceive you (verse 10). The kings of Assyria have destroyed every land; did the gods of the nations save them? Where are the kings of Hamath, Arpad and Sepharvaim (verses 11-13)?
passages.hearers:
Hezekiah does what his father Ahaz never did. He goes into the house of the LORD and sends for the prophet. The picture in verse 3, children at the point of birth with no strength to deliver them, is a mother in labor too weak to give birth: the crisis has come and Judah has no strength of its own.

The setting is Sennacherib's campaign of 701 BC. Lachish, the major fortress southwest of Jerusalem, had fallen, and the Assyrian king moved on to Libnah.

Tirhakah, or Taharqa, was a ruler of Egypt's Twenty-Fifth Dynasty, whose kings came from Cush. Egyptian records suggest he did not become king until about 690 BC, so in 701 he was probably a young prince leading the army; most interpreters think the text calls him king by the title he later held, though some propose other solutions.

The Assyrian king's second message repeats the first boast: no god has ever saved a land from Assyria. He has put the LORD on the same level as the idols of the cities he destroyed.
passages.later: Kings tells the same scene in the same words: ‘On hearing this report, King Hezekiah tore his clothes, put on sackcloth, and entered the house of the LORD’ (2 Kings 19:1).
passages.asks: When the threat came, Hezekiah went into the house of the LORD and asked for prayer. Ask where you go first when the crisis comes. And ask who you would ask to pray for you when you have no strength left.

passages.t: A letter spread before the LORD
passages.happening:
‘So Hezekiah received the letter from the messengers, read it, and went up to the house of the LORD and spread it out before the LORD’ (verse 14).

He prays: ‘O LORD of Hosts, God of Israel, enthroned above the cherubim, You alone are God over all the kingdoms of the earth. You made the heavens and the earth’ (verse 16). ‘Incline Your ear, O LORD, and hear; open Your eyes, O LORD, and see’ (verse 17). Listen to the words Sennacherib has sent to defy the living God.

‘Truly, O LORD, the kings of Assyria have laid waste all these countries and their lands’ (verse 18). They threw their gods into the fire, ‘for they were not gods, but only wood and stone’ (verse 19). ‘And now, O LORD our God, save us from his hand, so that all the kingdoms of the earth may know that You alone, O LORD, are God’ (verse 20).
passages.hearers:
Hezekiah spreads the letter out before God, as if to say, read this. His prayer begins not with the danger but with who God is: enthroned above the cherubim of the ark, God alone over every kingdom, the maker of heaven and earth.

He is honest about the facts. Assyria really has destroyed the nations and their gods. But those gods were only wood and stone. The LORD is the living God, and Sennacherib has defied him.

The last line of the prayer asks for rescue not only for Judah's sake but so that every kingdom will know that the LORD alone is God. The first hearers were given a model of prayer in a crisis: name who God is, tell him the truth, and ask for his name's sake.
passages.later: Kings records the same prayer (2 Kings 19:15-19). And a psalm prays, ‘Help us, O God of our salvation, for the glory of Your name’ (Psalm 79:9).
passages.asks: Hezekiah spread the threatening letter out before God. Ask what letter, message or threat you need to spread before him today. And ask whether your prayers begin with who God is, or only with what you need.

passages.t: The Virgin Daughter of Zion mocks you
passages.happening:
Isaiah sends Hezekiah the LORD's answer: because you have prayed (verse 21), this is the word against Sennacherib. ‘The Virgin Daughter of Zion despises you and mocks you; the Daughter of Jerusalem shakes her head behind you’ (verse 22). “Whom have you taunted and blasphemed? Against whom have you raised your voice and lifted your eyes in pride? Against the Holy One of Israel!” (verse 23).

Sennacherib boasted of his chariots and his conquests (verses 24-25). But ‘Long ago I ordained it; in days of old I planned it’ (verse 26). His victories were God's doing all along. ‘I will put My hook in your nose and My bit in your mouth; I will send you back the way you came’ (verse 29).

A sign for Hezekiah: this year and next they will eat what grows of itself, and in the third year they will sow and reap (verse 30). ‘And the surviving remnant of the house of Judah will again take root below and bear fruit above’ (verse 31).

The king of Assyria ‘will not enter this city or shoot an arrow into it’ (verse 33). He will go back the way he came (verse 34). ‘I will defend this city and save it for My own sake and for the sake of My servant David’ (verse 35).
passages.hearers:
The answer comes because Hezekiah prayed. The besieged city, pictured as a young woman, is told to mock the great king as he retreats, shaking her head behind him.

Sennacherib's boast was that he had done it all by his own strength. God's answer is that he planned it long ago; the Assyrian was only a tool, and now the tool will be led home like an animal with a hook in its nose and a bit in its mouth. Assyrian kings did lead captives that way, and their reliefs show it. Now the same is done to the king.

The sign of verse 30 meant two years of living on what grew of itself, because the invading army had ruined the planting, and then a return to normal farming. The remnant will take root again, the promise of Shear-jashub's name kept.

The promise of verses 33 to 35 is exact. No arrow, no shield, no siege ramp at Jerusalem. Lachish had seen all three. Jerusalem would see none.
passages.later: Kings gives the same oracle (2 Kings 19:21-34). And Isaiah had promised long before, ‘A remnant will return’ (Isaiah 10:21).
passages.asks: God answered because Hezekiah prayed. Ask what you have not yet prayed about. And ask whether you can trust that the powers that frighten you are, in the end, led by God's hook and bit.

passages.t: The camp struck in a night
passages.happening:
‘Then the angel of the LORD went out and struck down 185,000 men in the camp of the Assyrians’ (verse 36). When the people got up in the morning, there were the dead bodies.

‘So Sennacherib king of Assyria broke camp and withdrew. He returned to Nineveh and stayed there’ (verse 37).

One day, as he worshiped in the temple of his god Nisroch, his sons Adrammelech and Sharezer killed him with the sword and escaped to the land of Ararat. ‘And his son Esar-haddon reigned in his place’ (verse 38).
passages.hearers:
The event is told in a few plain sentences, with no celebration. The people rose in the morning and found the dead.

Sennacherib's own annals claim a successful campaign, but they never claim to have captured Jerusalem or removed Hezekiah, which is striking for a king who routinely did both to rebels. His assassination in verse 38 took place in 681 BC, twenty years after the campaign. A Babylonian chronicle records that he was killed by his son in a rebellion, and Esarhaddon did succeed him. The god Nisroch has not been securely identified.

The king who mocked the LORD as one more powerless god was killed in the temple of his own god, who could not protect him.
passages.later: Kings records the same: ‘That very night the angel of the LORD went out and struck down 185,000 men in the camp of the Assyrians’ (2 Kings 19:35). Isaiah had foretold that Assyria would fall ‘but not by the sword of man’ (Isaiah 31:8).
passages.hard:
Did an angel really kill 185,000 Assyrian soldiers in one night, and what does history say?

The difficulty is real on two fronts: the number of dead, and the lack of any Assyrian record of disaster. Assyrian royal inscriptions did not report defeats, so their silence is expected. What they do show is that Sennacherib never claims to have taken Jerusalem or deposed Hezekiah. The Greek historian Herodotus, writing in the fifth century BC, preserves an Egyptian story that Sennacherib's army withdrew after mice gnawed its equipment in the night, which some connect with a plague. Many interpreters who read the account as history think God used an epidemic in the camp; others take the text as describing a direct act of God. Some scholars read the number and the angel as a later heightening of a real, unexpected withdrawal. Readers also debate whether the Hebrew word for thousand here can mean a military unit, which would lower the figure, though this is uncertain.

The text presents the event not as random slaughter but as God's judgment on an empire that had destroyed nation after nation and now openly defied him. It is told soberly, with no celebration. These notes take no side among the readings, and they find in the chapter no reason to rejoice over anyone's death.
passages.asks: The king who mocked God as powerless was struck down in his own god's temple. Ask what powers you have feared that are less than they seem. And ask how you can receive God's rescue without delighting in anyone's destruction.
